entries.title: Note deleted by actor stranger, which the spec denies
entries.detail: DELETE /api/notes/N-1 as actor stranger returned 200 with no Note fields, and Note N-1 was readable before the request and is absent after it. Request: DELETE /api/notes/N-1. Evidence: EV-00000b. Suggestion: in the DELETE /api/notes/{id} handler, check the rule condition Note.owner_id != actor.user_id before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: The application this corpus missed entirely at S8, now caught. A stranger deleted nora's note: N-1 was readable before the request and gone after it, which is the record rather than the response settling it. NOTES.md says anybody signed in can delete anybody's note, and AR-003-01 denies exactly that. The 200 carried no fields, which is why the old verdict table could only say it did not know.

entries.title: Note readable by actor anonymous, which the spec denies
entries.detail: GET /api/notes/NOTE-2 as actor anonymous returned 200 with Note fields body, id, owner_id, shared. Request: GET /api/notes/NOTE-2. Evidence: EV-000007. Suggestion: in the GET /api/notes/{id} handler, check the caller identity before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: An anonymous caller read NOTE-2 and got the body. AR-004-01 denies an anonymous read unconditionally, and REQ-004 says a shared note is readable by anyone signed in and only by someone signed in. NOTES.md names this exact request as what a run should find. The access family missed it before because NOTE-1 is tried first and is correctly refused with a 401.

entries.title: Note readable by actor other, which the spec denies
entries.detail: GET /api/notes/NOTE-2 as actor other returned 200 with Note fields body, id, owner_id, shared. Request: GET /api/notes/NOTE-2. Evidence: EV-000005. Suggestion: in the GET /api/notes/{id} handler, check the rule condition Note.owner_id != actor.user_id before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: The application is behaving as its own spec intends and still violates a rule that spec states. Erin read NOTE-2, which is dana's and is marked shared. REQ-004 says a shared note is readable by anyone signed in, and erin is signed in, so NOTES.md would call this correct. AR-001-01 denies erin reading any note whose owner is not erin, with no exception for shared, so the rule as written is violated and the report is accurate about it. The disagreement is between REQ-001 and REQ-004 rather than between the spec and the application, and deciding which one is wrong is the spec author's call, not the reviewer's. Left unclear deliberately: calling it a true positive would claim the application is broken, and calling it a false positive would claim the tool misread a rule it read correctly.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-004-01
entries.detail: GET /api/notes/NOTE-2 as actor anonymous returned status 200, Note.body in the body. The criterion requires: status in 401, 403 and body omits field Note.body.
entries.note: The planted defect, caught exactly. The shared branch returns the note before the caller is resolved, so an unauthenticated caller reads NOTE-2. The finding names the request, the actor, the status, and what the criterion required.

entries.title: fields of Note disagree between the spec and the target
entries.note: Note.owner_id and Note.body are both returned by GET /api/notes/{id}. The probe only reached the listing, which returns id and shared, so the fields it never saw are reported as specified and not observed. That is the crawl's coverage being reported as a fact about the application.

entries.title: fields of Booking disagree between the spec and the target
entries.note: Booking.cancelled is returned and the spec declares no such field. The spec was written from the prompt, which says a booking can be cancelled and never says a record carries the fact, and the application chose to mark rather than remove. Genuinely undeclared, and the second structural field finding in the corpus that is right. Both of them are the observed side, which is the side S8.6 deliberately left alone.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-003-01
entries.detail: POST /api/bookings as actor anonymous returned status 201. The criterion requires: status is 401.
entries.note: AC-003-01. An unsigned caller created a booking and got 201 where the criterion requires 401. The behavioral half of the same defect the high severity access finding reports, from the status rather than from the fields.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-004-01
entries.detail: GET /api/bookings as actor anonymous returned status 200. The criterion requires: status is 401.
entries.note: AC-004-01. An unsigned caller listed the bookings and got 200 where the criterion requires 401. Worth noting beside it: the matching access rule came back inconclusive, correctly, because ownership of the returned rows could not be established from the rule condition. The criterion is what turned that into a finding, which is the argument for having both families.

entries.title: Booking deleted by actor colleague, which the spec denies
entries.detail: DELETE /api/bookings/B-1 as actor colleague returned 200 with no Booking fields, and Booking B-1 was readable before the request and is absent after it. Request: DELETE /api/bookings/B-1. Evidence: EV-000007. Suggestion: in the DELETE /api/bookings/{id} handler, check the rule condition Booking.booked_by != actor.user_id before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: B-1 was readable before the delete and absent after it, and AR-001-01 denies a colleague cancelling a booking they did not make. This application has no authentication at all, and its NOTES.md says every deny rule in its spec should produce a failed access check, so this is one of the ones that was missing.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-002-01
entries.detail: DELETE /api/bookings/B-2 as actor anonymous returned status 200. The criterion requires: status is 401.
entries.note: AC-002-01. An unsigned caller cancelled a booking and got 200 where the criterion requires 401. True against an application that authenticates nobody.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-001-01
entries.detail: DELETE /api/bookings/B-2 as actor colleague returned status 200. The criterion requires: status in 401, 403, 404.
entries.note: AC-001-01. "DELETE /api/bookings/B-2 as actor colleague returned status 200. The criterion requires: status in 401, 403, 404." A colleague cancelled somebody else's booking and the application allowed it. True, and it is the criterion rather than the access rule that caught it, because the access rule saw a 200 with no recognizable fields and declined.

entries.title: Booking readable by actor anonymous, which the spec denies
entries.detail: POST /api/bookings as actor anonymous returned 201 with Booking fields booked_by, id, room_id, starts_at. Request: POST /api/bookings. Evidence: EV-00000b. Suggestion: in the POST /api/bookings handler, check the caller identity before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: The only high severity access finding in the corpus, and it is right. "POST /api/bookings as actor anonymous returned 201 with Booking fields booked_by, id, room_id, starts_at." The application has no authentication at all, so an unsigned caller creates a booking. The finding names the actor, the request, the status, and the fields that came back, which is the shape 04-CONVENTIONS.md asks for.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-002-01
entries.detail: GET /api/documents as actor member returned Document.contents in the body. The criterion requires: body omits field Document.contents.
entries.note: The planted defect, caught exactly. One documentView was written for the download route and the directory route calls it too, so every file in the project is handed over in full to anyone who lists it. Nothing about the access rules is wrong and the finding does not claim otherwise: it is a field level claim about a listing, which is the only level this defect exists at.

entries.title: Message readable by actor outsider, which the spec denies
entries.detail: GET /api/messages/MSG-3 as actor outsider returned 200 with Message fields body, channel_id, id, team_id. Request: GET /api/messages/MSG-3. Evidence: EV-000005. Suggestion: in the GET /api/messages/{id} handler, check the rule condition Message.team_id != actor.team_id before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: The same read of MSG-3, reported against AR-001-01 as well, because REQ-001 and REQ-002 carry the identical condition: an access rule has nowhere to name which channel, which S8 recorded as a limit of the spec language. The rule as written is violated, so the report is accurate. Worth knowing that it changes the shape NOTES.md predicted, REQ-001 passing while REQ-002 fails, because that shape depended on only one instance being tried.

entries.title: Message readable by actor outsider, which the spec denies
entries.detail: GET /api/messages/MSG-3 as actor outsider returned 200 with Message fields body, channel_id, id, team_id. Request: GET /api/messages/MSG-3. Evidence: EV-000007. Suggestion: in the GET /api/messages/{id} handler, check the rule condition Message.team_id != actor.team_id before returning the record, and respond 404 rather than 403 so the response does not confirm that the record exists.
entries.note: The outsider read MSG-3 and got the body. MSG-3 is a direct message, team_id DM, and AR-002-01 denies a read where the team does not match. This is the defect NOTES.md names: direct messages were added as another kind of channel and the participant check was never written. Previously invisible to the access family because only MSG-1 was tried, which the application refuses correctly.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-002-01
entries.detail: GET /api/messages/MSG-3 as actor outsider returned status 200, Message.body in the body. The criterion requires: status in 403, 404 and body omits field Message.body.
entries.note: The planted defect, caught exactly. The outsider reads MSG-3, a direct message between two other people, and the body comes back. REQ-001 passing while REQ-002 fails is the shape that says the team rule works and the direct message rule was never written.

entries.title: StockLine list returned rows belonging to another owner
entries.detail: GET /api/stock as actor otherStaff returned 200 with 3 row(s), 2 of which the rule denies: SKU-1, SKU-2. Request: GET /api/stock. Evidence: EV-000005. Suggestion: scope the GET /api/stock handler so it returns only rows matching the rule condition StockLine.warehouse_id != actor.warehouse_id, filtering in the query rather than after fetching.
entries.note: The unscoped listing, named row by row: 2 of 3 rows belong to another warehouse.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-002-01
entries.detail: GET /api/stock as actor otherStaff returned 2 of 3 StockLine row(s) without warehouse_id equal to actor.warehouse_id, which is "WH-SOUTH": SKU-1, SKU-2. The criterion requires: every StockLine has warehouse_id equal to actor.warehouse_id.
entries.note: The planted defect, caught, and it had never been caught before. The listing returns every warehouse and the finding names the two foreign rows by id: "2 of 3 StockLine row(s) without warehouse_id equal to actor.warehouse_id, which is WH-SOUTH: SKU-1, SKU-2". This criterion had been silently unplannable since the application was written, because it said "every row has field" and the vocabulary is "every <Entity> has <field>". Fixing the wording is what made the check run at all.

entries.detail: PATCH /api/stock/SKU-1 as actor anonymous returned status 200, StockLine SKU-1 changed across the action: quantity. The criterion requires: status in 401, 403 and record StockLine SKU-1 is unchanged.
entries.note: The write path has no credential check. The finding also proves the state moved, which is what separates an accepted write from a refused one.

entries.title: endpoint GET /api/stock was observed and is specified nowhere
entries.note: REQ-002 is about listing StockLine and the config maps list to GET /api/stock, so the endpoint is specified and the tool says it is not. It fires here and not on GET /api/invoices because the entity name matching relates invoices to Invoice and cannot relate stock to StockLine. Medium severity, which makes it the most damaging of the three: it is the kind of confident wrong answer that teaches a reader to stop reading the category.

entries.title: Acceptance criterion AC-003-01
entries.detail: GET /api/courses/CRS-10 as actor otherLearner returned Enrolment.grade in the body. The criterion requires: status is 200 and body omits field Enrolment.grade.
entries.note: The planted defect, caught, and caught on a route that serves a different entity. Every enrolment access rule passes, correctly, because the enrolment routes are right. The grades leave through the course detail view, which embeds the roster. "GET /api/courses/CRS-10 as actor otherLearner returned Enrolment.grade in the body." That is the shape of leak that survives a review of the access rules, and the tool found it.
